edges.label: On 2 November 1917 Arthur Balfour sent his declaration to "Lord Rothschild" at 148 Piccadilly, and asked him to pass it to the Zionist Federation.
The letter was drafted by Weizmann, Sokolow and Sykes and signed by Balfour, the Foreign Secretary.

The Third Congress, at Haifa in December 1920, declared the Balfour Declaration null and void and created a nine-member Arab Executive Committee, with Musa Kazim al-Husseini as its chairman.

The Internal Security Section of the Justice Department, under Attorney General Robert Kennedy, ordered the American Zionist Council to register as an agent of a foreign principal under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
Twelve days after the declaration of independence, the provisional government headed by David Ben-Gurion issued an order establishing the Israel Defense Forces.
Eleven minutes after David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel in Tel Aviv, the United States extended de facto recognition.
In 1882 Rabbi Samuel Mohilever appealed to Edmond to save the failing colony at Rishon LeZion, and Edmond accepted the appeal.
Edmond began funding Rishon LeZion in 1882, months after its founding, when it was collapsing for want of water and agricultural knowledge.
From 1883 the settlers transferred Zikhron Ya'akov's assets to Edmond; the colony was named "in memory of Jacob," his father James.
Edmond funded Rosh Pinna in Upper Galilee from 1883.
Edmond funded Mazkeret Batya from 1883; it was named for his mother, Betty (Batya).
Edmond funded Ekron on the coastal plain from 1884.
Edmond funded Metulla, the northernmost colony, from 1896.
On his first visit, from 2 April 1887, Edmond toured Mikveh Israel, Jerusalem and the colonies; he and his wife arrived at Jaffa anonymously, and Hamelitz reported it at once.
At the end of 1899 (1900 in another account) Edmond transferred title to his colonies to the JCA with fifteen (or fourteen) million francs.
In 1893 Rothschild obtained building permits after an agreement with the Porte on how many houses could be built in his colonies and how many settlers could live in them.
In 1924 Edmond reorganized the JCA's Palestine branch as PICA and appointed his son James president for life.
Edmond was the youngest son of James Mayer de Rothschild of the Paris house.
James Armand was Edmond's son; his father introduced him to Chaim Weizmann.
After his 1914 visit Edmond drew closer to the Zionist Organization and, during and after the war, aided Weizmann and Sokolow (another reference account says he remained separate).
When the Jewish Agency was enlarged in 1929 Edmond was chosen its honorary president.
Edmond contributed funds to the establishment of the Hebrew University.
In 1954 Edmond's remains were carried to Haifa on a naval frigate and reburied at Ramat HaNadiv at a state funeral.
Ben-Gurion gave the eulogy at the 1954 state funeral and called Edmond "the builder of the Jewish Yishuv."
Near the end of the First World War James recruited volunteers for the Jewish battalions under General Allenby.
James and Weizmann built a close personal and working relationship.
James was involved in initiating the establishment of the Hebrew University.
James sat in the British House of Commons for sixteen years.
James was PICA's president for life from 1924.
PICA was wound up in 1957; James's will instructed it to transfer most of its land in Israel to the Jewish National Fund.
On 31 December 1958 PICA vested its rights to land in Syria and Lebanon in the State of Israel.
Dorothy de Rothschild was James Armand's wife.
After 1957 Dorothy chaired Yad Hanadiv, the Rothschild family charities in Israel.
Dorothy saw through her husband's gift of funds to build the Knesset.
Dorothy was a close friend of Chaim Weizmann.
Walter Rothschild was a close friend of Weizmann and worked with him on the draft; on 19 June 1917 Balfour asked the two of them to submit a formula.
Walter worked to formulate the draft declaration; its wording began with a draft formula he sent to Balfour on 18 July 1917.
Walter was the eldest son of Nathan "Natty," the first Baron Rothschild.
In June 1917 the United States sent Henry Morgenthau on a mission whose real purpose was to sound out whether Turkey could be detached from Germany.
At the talks from 4 July 1917 (Gibraltar), Weizmann represented Britain; the agents concluded the time was "not now ripe" to approach the Turkish leaders.
